clue.text: He has no backing in opera

parts.note: a man is a he, a male person

indicators.note: backing means the little word no is written back to front

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A singer complains that he has nobody supporting him in the opera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' reads as the subject of the sentence but supplies a piece. Manon is Massenet's opera, and Puccini wrote Manon Lescaut.
explanation.definitionFit: Massenet's opera of that name tells of the doomed girl Manon Lescaut.

clue.text: … but he in unusual surroundings founded Bart's

indicators.note: in, with surroundings, says one piece sits inside the other here

parts.note: unusual means rare
taken as written

explanation.surface: Following on from the previous clue, a man in strange circumstances established a London hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening dots tie the surface to the clue before it. Rahere was the twelfth-century courtier who founded St Bartholomew's Hospital ('Bart's') in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Rahere, a monk of Henry I's court, established the priory and hospital of St Bartholomew in 1123.

clue.text: According to accordingly Cowper it held no charms for Alexander Selkirk

definitions.text: According to accordingly Cowper it held no charms for Alexander Selkirk

parts.words: According to accordingly Cowper it held no charms for Alexander Selkirk
parts.note: Cowper's poem in the voice of the marooned Selkirk asks where are the charms sages have seen in the face of being utterly alone

explanation.walkthrough: William Cowper's verses supposedly written by Alexander Selkirk, the castaway behind Robinson Crusoe, open 'O Solitude! where are the charms'. The repeated 'accordingly' is a printing slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Being alone on a desert island was the castaway's lot, and the poem says it had no appeal for him.

clue.text: Do wrong not so frequently, becoming chaste

parts.note: to do wrong is to sin
not so frequently means less often, or less

explanation.surface: Advice to a sinner to cut back on misdeeds and so become pure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming' is a link word joining wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being free from wrongdoing is a sense of chaste, pure and blameless.

clue.text: Applicable to one of the family

explanation.surface: Something relevant to a member of the household.
explanation.definitionFit: Relevant or pertinent in relation to something, and also a kinsman such as an aunt or cousin.

clue.text: Sounds an indispensable accompaniment

parts.note: a musical term for a part that must be played, whose name sounds like the word obligatory

explanation.walkthrough: The Italian musical term names an accompanying part that is essential and not to be left out; it is the same root as English 'obligatory'.
explanation.definitionFit: In music it marks an instrumental part that is required, not optional.

clue.text: Gives goat a pain where horses and cattle thrive

indicators.note: gives, in the sense of yields or bends, tells us to rework these three words' letters

explanation.surface: Something gives a goat discomfort in ranching country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gives' signals an anagram of GOAT A PAIN. Patagonia, in southern Argentina and Chile, is famous for its ranches.
explanation.definitionFit: The South American region is known for its estancias raising sheep, cattle and horses.

clue.text: Peach of a singer?

parts.note: a peach dessert named after a famous Australian soprano, read as a peach of a singer

explanation.walkthrough: Peach Melba was created by Escoffier for the soprano Nellie Melba; 'a peach of a singer' also means a wonderful one.
explanation.definitionFit: The diva Dame Nellie gave her stage name to the peach-and-raspberry dessert.

clue.text: Architect bird

explanation.surface: An architect who is also a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Christopher of St Paul's Cathedral, and a tiny brown songbird.

clue.text: Obstacle often exaggerated to mountainous proportions

definitions.text: Obstacle often exaggerated to mountainous proportions

parts.words: Obstacle often exaggerated to mountainous proportions
parts.note: the idiom of making a mountain out of a small earth heap thrown up by a burrowing animal

explanation.walkthrough: It plays on the saying 'to make a mountain out of a molehill', to exaggerate a minor difficulty.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom treats the small heap of soil as a trivial problem blown up into a huge one.

clue.text: Friend to Engineer in fact

indicators.note: to means added onto, so the friend comes after the engineer

parts.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
a friend is an ally

explanation.surface: Someone who is a genuine friend to an engineer.
explanation.walkthrough: RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps.
explanation.definitionFit: Really and in fact both mean actually or truly.

clue.text: Issue of a prize bull that's got the hump?

indicators.note: issue of means letters coming out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: Asking whether the calf of a prize bull is a sulky one.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across priZE BUll. 'got the hump' is British slang for being in a sulk, but the zebu has a literal hump.
explanation.definitionFit: This Asian breed of ox carries a fatty hump over its shoulders.

clue.text: Capital gains to a Chilean complex

indicators.note: complex means intricate or tangled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Money made through a South American financial scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'complex' signals an anagram of GAINS TO A; 'Chilean' points to the country whose capital it is.
explanation.definitionFit: Santiago is the capital city of Chile.

clue.text: Truly deep construction, by all accounts

indicators.note: construction means the letters are built into a new form

explanation.surface: A building said to be genuinely profound.
explanation.walkthrough: 'construction' rearranges the letters of TRULY DEEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Both mean according to what people say or believe.

clue.text: Sat and fished!

explanation.surface: Someone sat and went fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a coinage: to have fished for the freshwater fish called perch.
explanation.definitionFit: Settled on a seat or ledge, as a bird does, and, read as a made-up verb, went angling for perch.

clue.text: Spicy Shakespearean con- Spirator a Scotsman?

definitions.note: spicy is an adjective, the answer the noun naming a spice

parts.note: Cinna is one of the conspirators against Caesar in Julius Caesar
mon is the Scots form of man

explanation.surface: Asking whether a Scottish plotter in Shakespeare is a spicy character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'con- Spirator' is 'conspirator' broken across a line. 'Mon' is the stereotyped Scots for 'man'.
explanation.definitionFit: The bark of a tropical tree used as a sweet, warming spice in baking.

clue.text: Gives evidence at trials

parts.note: trials are tests

explanation.surface: A witness speaks in court cases.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear witness or certify is to give evidence.

clue.text: Revealing a raconteur, perhaps

explanation.surface: A storyteller who gives things away.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word: a raconteur will tell a tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Something telltale gives a secret away, and a storyteller is literally one who recounts a yarn.

clue.text: Bloomer — and it could be a big one

indicators.note: could be means the letters may become something else when rearranged

explanation.surface: A blunder that might well be a large one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' suggests a mistake (British slang) but means a flowering plant; 'could be' rearranges A BIG ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloomer is anything that flowers, and this is a popular bedding plant.

clue.text: Where one paid at the gate to bring fish back?

definitions.text: Where one paid at the gate

explanation.surface: A gate where a toll is paid, and returning a fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word: to turn a pike (the fish) is to send it back.
explanation.definitionFit: A road with a toll gate, and, split in two, a phrase for returning a predatory freshwater fish.

clue.text: American composer canonised in Cornwall

explanation.surface: A US composer made a saint in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Ives was an American composer; St Ives is a town in Cornwall, the county at England's south-west tip.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles of that surname wrote experimental music, and a saint with that name gives a Cornish seaside town its name.

clue.text: Provided in the French spirit

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: le is the French for the
provided means on condition that, if

explanation.surface: Something supplied within the French spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirit as in liveliness or vitality, as in 'full of it'.

clue.text: Name of upstanding enemy

indicators.note: in a down clue upstanding means the words are read from the bottom upward

explanation.surface: The name of an honourable adversary.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'upstanding' reverses NAME OF.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic word for an adversary in war.

clue.text: Accumulations of better resources, perchance

parts.note: a better is one who bets; the combined stakes of gamblers form a fund, and chance plays on the football coupon

explanation.walkthrough: 'better' means one who bets, not 'superior'. The football pools are a British betting system on match results.
explanation.definitionFit: Pooled stakes are combined funds of gamblers, and the football coupon game bears the name.

clue.text: When noticed, enter and you may get a bite

definitions.text: When noticed, enter and you may get a bite

parts.words: When noticed, enter and you may get a bite
parts.note: a warning sign on a gate: if you see it and still go in, a guard animal may bite you

explanation.walkthrough: 'noticed' means read on a notice; the clue describes what happens to someone who ignores the sign.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the familiar gate sign warning visitors of a guard animal.

clue.text: See 25
Type of cutter aft of 24

indicators.note: aft means toward the back of a ship, so the referenced entry is read backward

parts.note: 24 refers to the entry at 24 down, gamblers' collective stakes

explanation.surface: A kind of vessel sailing behind another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aft' is a nautical word that fits the boat, and signals a reversal of the answer at 24 down.
explanation.definitionFit: A cutter is a single-masted sailing vessel, and this is a similar one-masted boat.

clue.text: Be ideally suited to produce

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for an adjective meaning able to produce

indicators.note: suited, as in fitted or dressed differently, signals the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice to be perfectly matched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suited' rearranges BE IDEALLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Capable of giving forth a crop or result, able to bear or generate.
